steps.name: Registry
steps.narration: Every engine registers itself: an id, a title, what kind it is, its topics and what it depends on. Seventeen foundation parts so far.

steps.name: Lookup
steps.narration: Lessons can look parts up by topic. Ask for "number" and you get the maths text renderer and the worked example stepper.

steps.name: Manifest
steps.narration: A lesson manifest is a list of steps. Each step names a component, a mode and a learning objective: here, fractions of amounts.

steps.name: Validate
steps.narration: Validation catches mistakes before pupils see them: F0-99 is not a real component, and "play" is not a mode.

steps.name: Fix
steps.narration: Point step 4 at F0-11 and use challenge mode. Now the manifest is valid.

steps.name: Load order
steps.narration: The registry works out the load order: shared parts like design tokens and events come before the engines that need them.

steps.name: Objectives
steps.narration: Each objective links to its steps, so a report can say how pupils did on O1 and O2 separately.

steps.name: Shell
steps.narration: The gallery shell is the frame every bank page sits in: a header, filters, a search box and a grid of engine tiles.
steps.prompt: What three parts does the shell have?

steps.name: From the registry
steps.narration: Tiles come straight from the registry, so a new engine appears in the gallery as soon as it registers. No hand-made lists.
steps.prompt: Where does the tile list come from?

steps.name: Filter
steps.narration: Topic chips filter the grid. Choose geometry and only the SVG primitives and the geometry canvas stay.
steps.prompt: How many geometry tools are there?

steps.name: Search
steps.narration: Search matches ids and titles: type "plot" and you get the axes and plotting primitive, F0-14.

steps.name: Topic layer
steps.narration: Switch the style layer to algebra and the accents turn gold. Same shell, different topic mood, no extra code.

steps.name: Status
steps.narration: Badges show what is built (tick) and what is planned (dotted circle): shape as well as colour, so it works for everyone.

steps.name: Print
steps.narration: For print the shell drops its glow and turns into a clean light catalogue a teacher can hand out.

steps.name: Question types
steps.narration: One engine, four question types: numeric, multiple choice, select-all and put-in-order. Every question carries its marks and objective.

steps.name: Mark
steps.narration: A quarter of 24 is 6. The marker compares the answer and awards the mark.

steps.name: Equivalent answers
steps.narration: 3/4, 0.75 and .75 are the same number, so all of them score. Pupils are not punished for a different form.

steps.name: Method marks
steps.narration: Three quarters of 24 is worth 2 marks. This pupil found 24 ÷ 4 = 6 but slipped: 6 × 3 is 18, not 16. M1 for the method, no A1.
steps.prompt: Why does the pupil get 1 mark?

steps.name: Misconceptions
steps.narration: An answer of 6 for three quarters is a known trap: it is only one quarter. The feedback names the slip, not just "wrong".

steps.name: By objective
steps.narration: Results group by objective. O1 is strong; O2, non-unit fractions, needs more work. The striped bar marks the gap.

steps.name: Report
steps.narration: Marks, method credit, misconception notes and objective scores: everything a teacher needs, with no scores turned into games here.

steps.name: Wrap
steps.narration: The game wrapper sits around any engine. Engines just say right or wrong; the wrapper adds rounds, score, lives and hints.
steps.prompt: Who keeps the score: the engine or the wrapper?

steps.name: Score
steps.narration: 3/4 of 24 is 18. Correct: plus 10 points.
steps.prompt: How many points for a correct answer?

steps.name: Streak
steps.narration: 2/5 of 30 is 12. Two in a row starts a streak, worth a 5 point bonus.

steps.name: Lives
steps.narration: 1/3 of 27 is 9, not 8. No points, the streak resets and one life is lost.

steps.name: Hints
steps.narration: A hint costs 5 points. Helpful, never free, never a punishment that ends the game.

steps.name: Reactions
steps.narration: 5/8 of 40 is 25. Bob and the helper react to every answer, with poses that change for right and wrong.
steps.prompt: Which pose shows for a right answer?

steps.name: Results
steps.narration: At the end: score, percentage, stars and best streak. Four out of five is 80 percent: two stars.

steps.name: I do: set up
steps.narration: I do: I solve one while you watch. First, write the equation: 3x + 5 = 20.

steps.name: I do: undo +5
steps.narration: Subtract 5 from both sides to undo the plus 5. That leaves 3x = 15. Each line has its reason beside it.

steps.name: I do: undo ×3
steps.narration: Divide both sides by 3: x = 5. Then check by substituting back. 3 times 5 plus 5 is 20.

steps.name: We do: blanks
steps.narration: We do: a similar one together. 4x − 3 = 17. Add 3 to both sides. What goes in the blank?

steps.name: We do: fade
steps.narration: 4x = 20. Now the reasons start to fade: you supply the why. Divide by 4 to get x.

steps.name: You do
steps.narration: You do: 2x + 7 = 19 on your own. No reasons, no blanks filled. Same steps as before.

steps.name: Check
steps.narration: Subtract 7, then divide by 2: x = 6. I do, we do, you do: support fades as confidence grows.

lines: Find one fifth: divide by the denominator.
Three fifths: multiply by the numerator.

steps.name: Axes
steps.narration: Every chart starts with axes and a scale. x goes across from −1 to 5; y goes up in steps of 2.

steps.name: Plot points
steps.narration: For y = 2x + 1: when x is 0, y is 1; x is 1, y is 3; x is 2, y is 5. Coordinates are (across, up).

steps.name: Line
steps.narration: The points line up, so join them with a straight line: y = 2x + 1.

steps.name: Gradient and intercept
steps.narration: Up 2 for every 1 across: the gradient is 2. The line crosses the y axis at 1: the intercept.

steps.name: Scatter
steps.narration: Scatter graphs show pairs of data. Taller pupils tend to have longer arm spans: positive correlation.

steps.name: Bars
steps.narration: Bar charts compare categories on one scale. Grape is the most popular, with 9 votes. Patterns tell the bars apart without colour.

steps.name: Read a value
steps.narration: To read a value, go up from x = 3 to the line, then across: y = 7.

steps.name: Table
steps.narration: A table of values lists x values and works out y for each. Here the rule is y = 3x − 2.
steps.prompt: What rule fills the y row?

steps.name: Fill
steps.narration: Substitute each x. When x is −1: 3 times −1 is −3, take 2 is −5.

steps.name: Differences
steps.narration: Look along the row: y goes up by 3 each time x goes up by 1. That constant difference is the gradient.

steps.name: Link to graph
steps.narration: Each column is a coordinate. Plot them and they line up on y = 3x − 2.

steps.name: Highlight
steps.narration: Highlight a column and its point lights up too: x = 2, y = 4 is the point (2, 4).

steps.name: Spot the error
steps.narration: If a value is wrong, the point jumps off the line. 5 should be 4: 3 times 2 is 6, take 2 is 4.

steps.name: Complete
steps.narration: Complete table, steady differences, points on a line: the table and the graph tell the same story.

steps.name: Snap grid
steps.narration: Points snap to the grid, so coordinates stay exact. A is at (1, 1), B at (8, 1), C at (3, 6).

steps.name: Lines
steps.narration: Join the points with line segments to make triangle ABC.

steps.name: Measure
steps.narration: The canvas measures each side. AB runs along the grid: 7 units. The slanted sides use Pythagoras behind the scenes.

steps.name: Angles
steps.narration: Each angle is measured at its vertex and marked with an arc.

steps.name: Angle sum
steps.narration: Add the three angles: always 180 degrees, whatever the triangle.
steps.prompt: What do the angles add to?

steps.name: Right angle
steps.narration: A right angle gets a square mark, not an arc. This is a 3, 4, 5 triangle.

steps.name: Straight line
steps.narration: Angles on a straight line also add to 180 degrees. Drag the points in Explore to test it.

steps.name: Why static
steps.narration: Animations are great on screen, but paper and old devices need a still version. Every engine keeps a static fallback.
steps.prompt: When would you need a static version?

steps.name: Snapshot
steps.narration: The renderer copies the live SVG, fixes its colours inline and turns it into a PNG image, with the same alt text.
steps.prompt: What file type is the snapshot?

steps.name: Print theme
steps.narration: Print swaps the dark glowing theme for white paper and black ink. Easier to read, kinder to the printer.
steps.prompt: Why switch to a light theme?

steps.name: Worksheet
steps.narration: A worksheet has a title, a name line, the seed and questions in two columns with space to answer.
steps.prompt: How many questions on this sheet?

steps.name: Seeds
steps.narration: Change the seed and you get a fresh sheet; keep it and you get the same questions every time, so a class can share one.
steps.prompt: What gives the same sheet again?

steps.name: Answer key
steps.narration: The answer key prints on its own page. 3/4 of 24 style questions, answers ready to mark.

steps.name: Export
steps.narration: Print it straight away or download a standalone sheet. No internet needed once it is saved.
